results.result: The study identified 7,459,709 union origins from 113 datasets across five techniques, but only 0.27% (20,250) were reproducibly identified as shared origins. Origin profiles from the same technique are more correlated with each other than across different techniques, indicating substantial method-specific variability.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C28-C30, and C94 collectively demonstrate extensive variability in origin identification across methods. The data analysis with PCA (C29) and pairwise correlations (C30) provides strong statistical support for method-specific clustering. The identification of only 20,250 shared origins from ~7.5 million union origins (C2, C28) is well-documented with clear methodology.

results.result: Shared origins show strong enrichment at transcriptionally active chromatin regions, with 21% overlapping promoters and substantially higher overlap rates with TF-binding hotspots, CTCF sites, and G-quadruplexes compared to union origins.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C43, C45-C47 provide consistent quantitative evidence from genomic annotation and overlap analyses (Figures 2c-g). The conclusion (C89) that shared origins are in epigenetically active chromatin with promoter preference is well-supported by the enrichment data. Citation C44 provides appropriate context from prior literature.

results.result: Only 6.4% of shared human origins are within 1 kb of reproducible ORC-binding sites, and only 3.11% of ORC-binding sites are proximal to shared origins, representing dramatically lower co-localization than the nearly 100% overlap observed in yeast.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C59-C64 provide consistent quantitative evidence from multiple analyses including genome-wide comparisons and cell line-specific analyses. The stark contrast with yeast (C6, C65) strengthens the finding. The conclusion (C91) is appropriately cautious about the low co-localization. Distance and overlap analyses are clearly documented in Figures 3f-g.

results.result: Only 4.5% of shared human origins are within 1 kb of MCM-binding sites, with similarly low overlap rates in cell line-specific analyses (3.8-19.5%), contrasting sharply with ~95% overlap in yeast.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C81-C84 provide consistent evidence from multiple MCM datasets and cell line-specific analyses. The comparison with yeast (C80) provides important context. The data are supported by proximity analyses shown in Figure 5g and supplementary figures. The low overlap is consistently observed across different MCM subunits.

results.result: BART analysis identified transcription factors and chromatin remodeling factors (PAF1, EZH2, ZNF282, POLR2A, GTF2I) associated with shared origins, and histone modification analysis revealed substantial enrichment of activating marks (H3K4me3, H3/H4ac) with modest enrichment of the repressive mark H3K27me3.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C50 are supported by BART analysis (Figure 2h) and comprehensive histone modification enrichment analysis using 5,711 ChIP-seq datasets (Figure 2i). The methodology for histone enrichment is clearly described. The paradoxical enrichment of both activating and repressive marks is appropriately noted and discussed.

results.result: The 1,300 'highest-confidence origins' (shared origins proximal to ORC-binding sites) show even greater co-localization with promoters, TF-binding hotspots, and CTCF sites compared to shared origins alone, and are associated with genes having higher expression levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C69, C74 provide consistent evidence for progressive enrichment of genomic features as origin confidence increases. The analyses shown in Figures 4a-c and 4g support these claims. The definition of 'highest-confidence origins' is clearly stated (C66), and the comparative analyses are appropriate.

results.result: 74 origins were reproducibly identified by multiple methods and are proximal to both ORC-binding sites and MCM-binding sites, representing the most stringently validated origins.
results.evaluation: Claim C88 is supported by Venn diagram analysis (Figure 5h) and the coordinates are provided in supplementary files. These represent the intersection of multiple stringent criteria and provide a high-confidence set for future experimental validation.

results.result: Permutation testing revealed that shared origins show statistically significant enrichment (3.5-fold) with G-quadruplexes above random background, greater than the enrichment of promoters with G-quadruplexes (1.3-fold), while enrichment with CTCF sites (4.3-fold) is comparable to promoters (4.5-fold).
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C102, C104, C106 are supported by rigorous permutation testing with 1,000 iterations (Table 2). The statistical methodology is appropriate and clearly described. The differential enrichment patterns between G-quadruplexes and CTCF sites provide important insights into potential origin specification mechanisms.

results.result: No clear clustering of origins by cell type was observed in PCA analysis, except for six SNS-seq datasets from CCRF-CEM T lymphoblasts performed by one group. SNS-seq reproducibility did not improve progressively from 2018 to 2022.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C34 are supported by PCA analyses shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c-e. The exception for CCRF-CEM cells (C33) is appropriately noted with citation. The lack of temporal improvement (C34) is an important negative result that is clearly documented.

results.result: In K562 cells, 48.9% of shared origins overlapped with SNS-seq origins, 19.1% with OK-seq IZs, and 5.7% with Repli-seq origins. Conversely, only 2.7% of SNS-seq origins, 17.2% of OK-seq IZs, and 7.7% of Repli-seq IZs overlapped with shared origins.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C54 provide important bidirectional overlap analysis in a single cell line (K562). The data are supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 2. This analysis reveals that while SNS-seq captures more shared origins, it also has a high false-positive rate, which is an important methodological insight.

results.result: Only 21% of ORC1 peaks overlapped with ORC2 peaks, and 68% of ORC1 peaks are ≥2 kb from the closest ORC2 peaks, suggesting ORC subunits may bind chromatin independently in human cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C87 are supported by overlap analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1a-b. The comparison with other protein complexes (SMC1A/SMC3, EZH2/SUZ12) provides important controls. This finding challenges the assumption that ORC subunits always bind as a complete complex and is supported by citations to prior experimental work (C112-C114).

results.result: 22% of shared origins are proximate to phospho-S108 MCM2-binding sites, showing better co-localization than total MCM2-7-binding sites.
results.evaluation: Claim C85 is supported by proximity analysis of phosphorylated MCM2 isoforms. This represents an improvement over total MCM binding and suggests that specific post-translational modifications may mark functionally active MCM complexes. The analysis is clearly documented though the improvement is still modest.

results.result: The enrichment of genomic features (G-quadruplexes, CTCF sites, ORC sites) near shared origins may be secondary to origins' proximity to promoters rather than directly specifying origins. Current ORC/MCM-binding sites should not be used as surrogate markers for origins, and improved methods are needed.
results.evaluation: Claims C90, C92-C93, C115 represent important interpretive conclusions, but the evidence is inherently correlative. While the permutation tests (C101-C106) provide statistical rigor, the causal relationships cannot be definitively established from the correlation data alone. The authors appropriately acknowledge this limitation (C115) and call for experimental validation. The conclusions are reasonable but require additional experimental work to confirm.

results.result: DNA replication initiates from approximately 50,000 origins on human chromosomes based on inter-origin distances of ~100 kb.
results.evaluation: Claim C1 is based on established knowledge and inference from inter-origin distances. This is a well-accepted estimate in the field and provides important context for interpreting the large number of origins identified in the study. The calculation is straightforward: 3 billion bp / 100 kb = ~30,000-50,000 origins.

results.result: Shared origins replicate earlier in S phase compared to union origins based on replication timing scores, but there is no significant difference in timing between shared origins that overlap or do not overlap with ORC-binding sites.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C73 are supported by replication timing analysis using the ENCODE pipeline (Figure 4f). The methodology is appropriately cited (C72). The finding that ORC proximity does not affect replication timing is an important negative result that challenges simple models of ORC function.

results.result: The extensive variation in origins between datasets is attributed to technical noise and extreme stochasticity of origin selection in individual cells and cell cycles.
results.evaluation: Claim C95 is speculative and represents one possible explanation for the observed variability. While the extensive variation is well-documented (C2, C94), the specific causes cannot be definitively determined from the data presented. Both technical noise and biological stochasticity likely contribute, but their relative contributions remain unclear. This is appropriately framed as speculation.

results.result: The authors analyzed 113 genome-wide origin datasets from five different techniques (SNS-seq, Repli-seq, Rerep-seq, OK-seq, Bubble-seq) and found that only 0.27% (20,250) of ~7.5 million union origins were reproducibly identified across datasets. PCA and correlation analyses showed that datasets from the same technique cluster together more than datasets from different techniques, with no clear clustering by cell type.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 raises fundamental concerns about the methodology, stating that 'the approach of combining diverse methods that monitor different objects related to DNA replication leads to a base dataset that is highly flawed' and that 'only SNS-seq can actually identify origins rather than initiation zones.' Reviewer 1 also criticizes giving 'equal weight to all datasets' when 'some earlier versions have significantly different technical designs.' Reviewer 2 questions 'how can these two [noise and stochasticity] be differentiated' and expresses concern about the inclusion/exclusion logic. The reviewers fundamentally challenge the validity of the meta-analysis approach.

results.result: The shared origins (20,250 high-confidence origins) show enrichment at gene promoters (21% overlap), TF-binding hotspots, constitutive CTCF sites, and have higher GC content and G-quadruplex overlap compared to union origins. They also show enrichment of activating histone marks (H3K4me3, H3/H4 acetylation) and association with transcription factors like PAF1, EZH2, ZNF282, POLR2A, and GTF2I.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 acknowledges that 'the authors show that high-confidence origins recapitulate several known features of origins (e.g., correspondence with open chromatin, overlap with transcriptional promoters, CTCF binding sites)' and notes that 'many of the major genomic features analyzed have already been found to be associated with origin sites.' Reviewer 3 states the work 'reaches a very similar conclusion of these previous studies' regarding chromatin features. While reviewers note these findings are not novel, they do not dispute their validity.

results.result: The authors report surprisingly low overlap between shared origins and ORC-binding sites: only 6.4% of shared origins are within 1 kb of ORC-binding sites, and only 1.7% directly overlap. Even in cell line-matched data (K562, HeLa), overlaps remain low (12.8% and 6.1% respectively). Additionally, only 21% of ORC1 peaks overlap with ORC2 peaks, and 68% of ORC1 peaks are ≥2 kb from the closest ORC2 peak.
results.evaluation: This is the most contentious finding. The Editor notes 'the lack of overlap between binding sites for ORC1 and ORC2, which are known to form a complex in human cells, is a particular concern and points to the evidence for the accurate localization of their binding sites in the genome being incomplete.' Reviewer 1 states 'if true, a clear lack of colocalization of ORC and origins would be a striking finding' but questions whether the data support this conclusion. Reviewer 2 expresses being 'on the fence about how much existing datasets are "junk" vs how much the prevailing hypothesis about replication needs to be revisited' and notes 'the key missing dataset is ORC1 and ORC2 CHiP-seq from the same cell type.' Reviewer 3 acknowledges the finding but notes 'this is most certainly not the case in metazoans where it has already been reported that chromatin bindings sites of ORC and Mcm2-7 do not necessarily overlap.'

results.result: The authors report similarly low overlap between shared origins and MCM-binding sites: only ~4.5% of shared human origins are within 1 kb of MCM-binding sites, compared to ~95% in yeast. Cell line-specific analyses show 3.8-5.5% overlap with MCM3-7 in K562 cells and 19.5% with MCM2 in HCT116 cells. Phospho-S108 MCM2 showed the best overlap at 22%.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 notes 'the resolution and the overlap of the MCM Chip-seq datasets is poor' and states 'I am not at all persuaded' by the conclusions. Reviewer 2 expresses concern about 'the lack of overlap with MCM' and states 'if true, these are potentially major discoveries that butts heads with numerous other studies that have suggested otherwise.' Reviewer 3 notes that 'Mcm2-7 is loaded in excess and thus only a fraction of Mcm2-7 would be predicted to coincide with replication start sites,' suggesting the low overlap may be expected rather than surprising.

results.result: In yeast S. cerevisiae, nearly 100% of shared origins overlap with ORC-binding sites and ~95% are close to MCM sites, in stark contrast to the low overlap observed in human cells.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not dispute the yeast data, which serves as a positive control. Reviewer 1 acknowledges the contrast between yeast and human systems. The yeast findings are used by all reviewers as a reference point for evaluating the human data, and no concerns are raised about the yeast analysis itself.

results.result: The authors identify 1,300 'highest-confidence origins' (shared origins proximate to ORC-binding sites) that show even stronger co-localization with promoters, TF-binding hotspots, and CTCF sites compared to shared origins alone. These origins are associated with higher gene expression levels and replicate earlier in S phase. Only 74 origins were identified near both ORC and MCM binding sites.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 states 'the method for identification of strong origins is not robust and of insufficient resolution' and questions the validity of this subset analysis. The small number of origins (74) that meet all criteria is not specifically discussed by reviewers, but the overall methodological concerns raised by Reviewer 1 cast doubt on these refined subsets. Reviewer 3 notes the analysis is 'comprehensive' but lacks 'novel biological insight.'

results.result: The authors conclude that shared origins represent only a small subset of all origins, are located in epigenetically active chromatin with preference for promoters, and that the extensive variation between datasets is due to technical noise and stochasticity of origin selection. They recommend that ORC/MCM binding sites should not be used as surrogate markers for origins in human cells.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 fundamentally disagrees with the conclusions, stating 'I do not find the authors responses sufficiently compelling to change my mind about the significance of the study or veracity of the conclusions.' Reviewer 2 remains 'on the fence' about whether the conclusions reflect dataset quality issues or genuine biology. Reviewer 3 acknowledges the conclusions are 'thought-provoking' but notes 'the major weakness of this paper is the lack of novel biological insight' and that the findings are 'already widely appreciated in the field.' The Editor expresses 'concerns regarding the conclusion that there might be alternative mechanisms.'

results.result: Permutation testing shows that overlap of shared origins with promoters, G-quadruplexes, R-loops, and CTCF-binding sites are all significantly above background. However, promoters also show significant overlap with these same features, making it unclear whether these features independently specify origins or are simply enriched because origins are near promoters.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge the statistical analysis or the permutation testing approach. The finding that these associations exist but may be confounded by promoter proximity is acknowledged as a limitation by the authors themselves and is not disputed by reviewers. This represents a methodologically sound analysis even if it doesn't resolve the mechanistic question.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on claims C101, C102, C104, C106. Both OpenEval and peer reviewers support the statistical analysis using permutation testing for G-quadruplexes and CTCF sites. The methodology is not disputed by either evaluation.

Strong disagreement on claims C2, C28-C30, C94. OpenEval finds the variability analysis well-supported with strong statistical evidence. Peer reviewers fundamentally challenge the meta-analysis approach, questioning whether combining diverse methods is valid and whether equal weighting is appropriate.

Major disagreement on claims C4, C59-C64, C91 regarding ORC-origin co-localization. OpenEval finds the low overlap well-documented and supported. Peer reviewers express serious concerns, with the Editor noting this as 'a particular concern' and reviewers questioning data quality and whether conclusions are justified.

Disagreement on claims C81-C84 regarding MCM-origin overlap. OpenEval finds consistent evidence across multiple datasets. Peer reviewers question the resolution and quality of MCM ChIP-seq data, with Reviewer 1 stating 'I am not at all persuaded' and Reviewer 2 noting potential conflict with other studies.

Partial agreement on claims C3, C43-C47 regarding chromatin features. OpenEval finds evidence well-supported. Peer reviewers acknowledge validity but note lack of novelty, with Reviewer 2 stating these features 'have already been found to be associated with origin sites.'

Disagreement on claims C66-C69, C74 regarding high-confidence origin enrichment. OpenEval finds progressive enrichment well-supported. Peer reviewers question the robustness of the method for identifying strong origins and note lack of novel biological insight.

Both uncertain but for different reasons on claims C90, C92-C93. OpenEval rates as uncertain due to correlative nature of evidence but finds conclusions reasonable. Peer reviewers fundamentally disagree with conclusions, questioning whether findings reflect data quality issues versus genuine biology.

Disagreement on claims C32-C34 regarding PCA clustering by method. OpenEval supports the findings as clearly documented. These claims are part of the broader methodological concerns raised by peer reviewers who question the validity of combining diverse methods.

Agreement on claims C48-C50 regarding histone modifications. OpenEval finds the enrichment analysis well-supported. Peer reviewers acknowledge these chromatin features as valid findings, though note they are not novel discoveries.

Disagreement on claims C86-C87 regarding ORC subunit overlap. OpenEval finds the low overlap between ORC1/ORC2 well-supported and striking. This finding is part of the broader ORC-origin concerns raised by peer reviewers, with the Editor specifically noting this as 'a particular concern.'

Disagreement on claim C85 regarding phosphorylated MCM2. OpenEval finds this represents an improvement in proximity analysis. This is part of the broader MCM analysis that peer reviewers question, with concerns about resolution and overlap of MCM ChIP-seq datasets.

Both address claims C72-C73 regarding replication timing. OpenEval supports this as an important negative result with appropriate methodology. This analysis is part of the high-confidence origin characterization that peer reviewers question for methodological robustness.

Both uncertain on claim C95 regarding causes of variability. OpenEval appropriately frames this as speculation. Peer reviewers remain 'on the fence' about whether variability reflects technical issues versus biological reality, questioning the fundamental interpretation.

Disagreement on claim C88 regarding 74 highest-confidence origins. OpenEval finds this high-confidence set well-supported for validation. This is part of the refined subset analysis that peer reviewers question for methodological robustness and insufficient resolution.
OpenEval supports claim C1 regarding estimated 30,000-50,000 origins in human genome as well-accepted field knowledge. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for this contextual claim.

OpenEval supports claims C51-C54 regarding bidirectional overlap analysis in K562 cells, finding important methodological insights about SNS-seq false-positive rates. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.

Peer reviewers support yeast data (claims C6, C65, C80) as valid positive control, acknowledging contrast with human systems. No specific OpenEval result addresses yeast findings in isolation, though yeast comparisons appear in other OpenEval results (R3, R4).
